trails.trailTip: Follow the red diamond markers out and back over repeated 60-ft dunes, carry at least a gallon of water per person (turn back when half is gone), don't start if it's 85°F or hotter, turn around if you can't see the next marker in blowing sand, and be off the trail by sunset — and as of October 2026, per NPS.gov, missile tests on the surrounding range can close Dunes Drive for up to three hours, so check the park's military-testing closure schedule before you go.
trails.didYouKnow: Alkali Flat is the dry bed of ancient Lake Otero, and the route is marked only by red diamond posts since footprints vanish quickly in the wind-blown gypsum sand.

trails.bestSeason: Year-Round (best at sunrise/sunset in summer heat)
trails.trailTip: Interpretive markers along this loop explain how plants and animals like the kit fox and bleached earless lizard survive on the shifting gypsum dunes — a good first stop before attempting a longer dune hike.
trails.didYouKnow: Several species here, including the bleached earless lizard, evolved lighter coloring in just a few thousand years to match the unusually white gypsum sand.

trails.trailTip: This flat 0.4-mile round-trip boardwalk is the park's only fully wheelchair- and stroller-accessible trail, with interpretive exhibits on dune geology, plants, and animals plus a shade canopy and benches — a good midday option when longer dune hikes are too hot.
trails.didYouKnow: This wheelchair- and stroller-accessible boardwalk was built to protect the fragile interdune crust that supports plant life between the shifting dunes.

trails.trailTip: Follow the orange spade markers around this 2-mile loop over 40-50 ft dunes, allow at least two hours, and bring a gallon of water per person plus sun protection since there's no shade or water in the dunefield — it's also a great spot to catch the sunset.
trails.didYouKnow: The loop connects a set of primitive campsites tucked between dunes, offering one of the only places in the National Park System to camp inside an active dunefield.

trails.trailTip: The seasonal playa is usually dry and cracked, but can hold a thin sheet of water after winter rains — stay on the marked path to avoid sinking into soft mud near the edges.
trails.didYouKnow: A playa is a temporary lakebed that fills only after significant rain, and this one gives a small preview of the much larger Lake Lucero basin nearby.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, ranger-led Lake Lucero tours run only about once a month from November through March and require an advance reservation through Recreation.gov, since the site is not open for independent access.
trails.didYouKnow: Lake Lucero is the source of the entire dunefield — selenite crystals dissolve here, and the wind-borne gypsum grains eventually pile up as the white dunes seen throughout the rest of the park.

trails.bestSeason: Year-Round (Fri-Sun evenings, start time shifts with sunset)
trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov, this free ranger-led walk of about half a mile runs Friday through Sunday evenings year-round, meeting at the signed Sunset Stroll parking area just past the Backcountry Camping Loop trailhead; no reservations are taken, and it's canceled during heat advisories, bad weather, or missile range activity, so confirm that day's start time with the visitor center.
trails.didYouKnow: This ranger-led walk is timed to end right as the sun sets behind the San Andres Mountains, lighting the gypsum dunes in shades of pink and gold.

trails.trailTip: This short walk near the picnic area is a good spot to safely photograph soaptree yuccas without leaving the developed part of the park — a great option on days with extreme heat warnings.
trails.didYouKnow: Soaptree yuccas can grow their stems fast enough to keep pace with a rising dune, sometimes ending up more than 20 feet tall as measured from their buried base.

animals.whereToLook: Sandy open areas near the Dune Life Nature Trail
animals.viewingTip: Scan the sand a few feet ahead rather than reaching toward a lizard you spot — their pale coloring is a camouflage adaptation to gypsum sand, and getting too close will send them darting into a burrow.
animals.didYouKnow: This lizard's bleached coloration evolved in only a few thousand years, one of the fastest documented cases of adaptive color change in a vertebrate.

animals.whereToLook: Small burrow entrances and paw prints in stabilized sand near dune edges, especially at dawn
animals.viewingTip: If you spot a den entrance, admire it and any nearby tracks from several yards away rather than approaching or peering inside — kit foxes are easily stressed out of a den, and a distant light after dark lets you watch without disturbing them.
animals.didYouKnow: Kit foxes are one of the smallest fox species in North America and can get most of the water they need from the moisture in their prey, rarely needing to drink.

animals.whereToLook: Grasslands bordering the dunefield near the park entrance road
animals.viewingTip: Pronghorn are easily spooked by vehicles stopping abruptly — pull fully off the road before watching or photographing a herd, and use binoculars rather than approaching on foot.
animals.didYouKnow: Pronghorn can sustain speeds of around 55 mph, making them the fastest land mammal in the Western Hemisphere.

animals.whereToLook: Along park roads and the Dune Life Nature Trail, often seen sprinting across sand
animals.viewingTip: Roadrunners are naturally curious and may approach visitors on their own — resist the urge to feed them, since human food makes them dependent and more likely to linger dangerously close to roads.
animals.didYouKnow: A roadrunner's distinctive X-shaped footprint, with two toes pointing forward and two back, made it hard for early trackers to tell which direction the bird was heading.

animals.whereToLook: Nearby wetlands and agricultural fields visible from the park entrance road during migration
animals.viewingTip: Watch migrating flocks from a distance with binoculars or a spotting scope rather than walking toward a feeding group — cranes are wary birds and will fly off if approached too closely.
animals.didYouKnow: Sandhill cranes are among the oldest living bird species, with a fossil record stretching back roughly 2.5 million years.

animals.whereToLook: Open dune edges and grasslands near the entrance road
animals.viewingTip: Never feed a coyote, even one that seems tame — a fed coyote quickly loses its fear of people and becomes a safety risk; enjoy a sighting from your car or a distance with binoculars instead.
animals.didYouKnow: White Sands' coyotes hunt kangaroo rats and other small mammals largely by sound, since their prey is most active after dark.

animals.whereToLook: Flowering desert shrubs bordering the dunefield, especially near the visitor center
animals.viewingTip: This wasp has one of the most painful stings of any insect in North America — watch it foraging on flowers from a step or two away rather than swatting at it or trying to handle it, and it will generally ignore you in return.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite the painful sting, tarantula hawks are not aggressive toward people and reserve their venom for paralyzing tarantulas to provision their young.

animals.whereToLook: Grasslands and dune edges bordering the park, most often seen at a distance
animals.viewingTip: Oryx are large with long, sharp horns and are not native to the area — admire them from your vehicle or with binoculars rather than approaching on foot, since they can behave unpredictably if cornered.
animals.didYouKnow: Oryx were introduced to the nearby White Sands Missile Range from Africa in 1969 for sport hunting and have since spread into the surrounding Tularosa Basin, including areas near the park.
